notes.heading: Overview
points: Architecture reflects cultural, religious, and historical evolution of India
Developed across ancient, medieval, and modern periods
Major styles include Indus Valley, Mauryan, Gupta, Temple, Islamic, and Colonial architecture
Serves as key source for understanding political and social history

notes.heading: Indus Valley Civilization Architecture
points: Well-planned cities like Harappa and Mohenjo-daro
Grid pattern layout with streets intersecting at right angles
Advanced drainage system (covered drains)
Use of baked bricks (standardized ratio 1:2:4)
Important structures: Great Bath (Mohenjo-daro), Granary, Assembly halls

notes.heading: Mauryan Architecture
points: Marked by royal patronage of Ashoka
Use of stone instead of wood (shift in material culture)
Ashokan pillars with polished surface and animal capitals
Stupas like Sanchi Stupa (Buddhist relic structures)
Rock-cut architecture beginnings (Barabar Caves)

notes.heading: Gupta Architecture
points: Considered the 'Golden Age' of Indian art and architecture
Emergence of temple architecture (early Hindu temples)
Nagara style beginnings in North India
Examples: Dashavatara Temple (Deogarh), brick temples of Bhitargaon
Development of intricate carvings and iconography

notes.heading: Temple Architecture Styles
points: Nagara Style (North India) – curvilinear shikhara
Dravida Style (South India) – pyramid-shaped vimana, gopurams
Vesara Style (Deccan) – hybrid of Nagara and Dravida
Temple components: Garbhagriha, Mandapa, Shikhara/Vimana, Amalaka

notes.heading: Islamic Architecture in India
points: Introduced during Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods
Features: domes, arches, minarets, geometric designs
Use of calligraphy and arabesque decoration
Important monuments: Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza, Taj Mahal
Blend of Persian, Central Asian, and Indian styles (Indo-Islamic architecture)

notes.heading: Mughal Architecture
points: Peak of Indo-Islamic architecture
Use of red sandstone and white marble
Charbagh (four-fold garden layout)
Symmetry and grandeur emphasized
Important structures: Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Fatehpur Sikri

notes.heading: Colonial Architecture
points: Developed under British rule
Fusion of European styles (Gothic, Neo-Classical, Indo-Saracenic)
Important buildings: Rashtrapati Bhavan, Victoria Memorial, Gateway of India
Railway stations and administrative buildings built on grand scale
Indo-Saracenic style combined Indian motifs with Gothic structure

notes.heading: Important Features for UPSC
points: Indus Valley = urban planning + drainage system
Mauryan = stone architecture + pillars
Gupta = temple architecture beginnings
Mughal = symmetry + gardens + marble
Indo-Saracenic = British + Indian fusion style

notes.heading: Overview
points: Harappan Civilization (Indus Valley Civilization) existed around 2600 BCE – 1900 BCE
One of the earliest urban civilizations in the world
Flourished in present-day India, Pakistan, and Afghanistan
Known for advanced town planning, trade, and standardized culture
Major sites: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Dholavira, Lothal, Kalibangan

notes.heading: Geographical Extent
points: Western boundary: Sutkagendor (Pakistan-Iran border)
Eastern boundary: Alamgirpur (Uttar Pradesh)
Northern boundary: Manda (Jammu & Kashmir)
Southern boundary: Daimabad (Maharashtra)
Core region: Punjab, Sindh, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana

notes.heading: Town Planning Features
points: Grid pattern city layout with perpendicular streets
Divided into Citadel (upper town) and Lower town
Well-planned drainage system with covered drains
Standardized baked bricks in 1:2:4 ratio
Houses built with courtyard system and multiple rooms

notes.heading: Important Cities and Features
points: Harappa – first discovered site; granaries
Mohenjo-daro – Great Bath, advanced urban planning
Dholavira – water conservation system, inscriptions
Lothal – dockyard, trade center
Kalibangan – evidence of ploughed field, fire altars

notes.heading: Economic Life
points: Agriculture: wheat, barley, cotton (first cotton cultivation)
Trade: internal and external (Mesopotamia)
Standardized weights and measures
Crafts: bead-making, pottery, metallurgy
No evidence of coinage system

notes.heading: Religious Practices
points: No clear evidence of temples
Worship of Mother Goddess
Pashupati seal (proto-Shiva figure)
Worship of animals, trees (Peepal tree sacred)
Ritual bathing (Great Bath significance)

notes.heading: Art and Architecture
points: Terracotta figurines and pottery designs
Beads made of semi-precious stones
Seals made of steatite with animal motifs
Bronze sculpture: Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro
Highly developed urban craftsmanship

notes.heading: Important Features for UPSC
points: Oldest urban civilization in India
No evidence of iron use
No large temples or palaces found
Script is undeciphered
Highly organized civic administration

notes.heading: Overview
points: Mauryan Architecture (c. 322 BCE – 185 BCE) represents the first major imperial architecture in India
Developed under Mauryan rulers, especially Ashoka
Marked shift from wood-based to stone architecture
Strong association with Buddhism, especially under Ashoka
Known for pillars, stupas, caves, and polished stone structures

notes.heading: Key Features of Mauryan Architecture
points: Use of highly polished sandstone (Mauryan polish)
Monumental scale and imperial patronage
Religious influence mainly Buddhist (later Hindu and Jain also)
Use of inscriptions (Ashokan edicts)
Beginnings of rock-cut architecture in India

notes.heading: Ashokan Pillars
points: Erected by Emperor Ashoka across the empire
Made of single sandstone blocks (monolithic)
Polished surface known as Mauryan polish
Inscriptions in Brahmi script (Prakrit language)
Famous animal capitals like Lion Capital (Sarnath)

notes.heading: Important Stupas
points: Stupas are dome-shaped Buddhist structures containing relics
Ashoka is credited with building many stupas
Most famous: Sanchi Stupa (originally built by Ashoka, later expanded)
Hemispherical dome symbolizing universe
Surrounded by railings (vedika) and gateways (toranas)

notes.heading: Rock-Cut Architecture
points: Earliest examples of rock-cut caves in India
Barabar Caves in Bihar are finest examples
Dedicated mainly to Ajivika sect
Highly polished interior surfaces
Represents technical excellence in stone carving

notes.heading: Mauryan Sculpture
points: Highly refined and polished stone sculptures
Lion Capital of Sarnath is the national emblem of India
Bull capital at Rampurva
Yaksha and Yakshini figures (folk deities)
Blend of royal and religious themes

notes.heading: Important Sites

Sanchi – Great Stupa
Barabar Hills – Rock-cut caves
Rampurva – Ashokan pillar with bull capital
Lauriya Nandangarh – Ashokan pillar site

notes.heading: Overview
points: Post-Mauryan period (c. 200 BCE – 300 CE) saw regional kingdoms and cultural diversification
Major dynasties: Shungas, Kanvas, Satavahanas, Kushanas, and Western Kshatrapas
Marked development in Buddhist art, sculpture, and early temple architecture
Two major schools of art emerged: Gandhara and Mathura
Increased influence of foreign cultures like Greeks, Central Asians, and Parthians

notes.heading: Shunga and Kanva Dynasties
points: Shungas (c. 185–73 BCE) succeeded Mauryas in North India
Revival of Brahmanical traditions alongside Buddhism
Development of Bharhut Stupa and expansion of Sanchi Stupa
Kanvas followed Shungas but ruled for a short period
Art was mainly Buddhist with decorative railings and gateways

notes.heading: Satavahana Period
points: Ruled Deccan and Central India (c. 1st century BCE – 3rd century CE)
Important rulers: Gautamiputra Satakarni
Patrons of Buddhism and early rock-cut architecture
Ajanta caves (early phase) and Karle caves developed
Use of Prakrit language and Brahmi script

notes.heading: Kushana Empire
points: Central Asian origin dynasty (c. 1st–3rd century CE)
Important ruler: Kanishka
Promoted Mahayana Buddhism
Major centers: Mathura and Gandhara
Issued gold coins and promoted trade along Silk Route

notes.heading: Gandhara School of Art
points: Developed in present-day Afghanistan and North-West India
Strong Greco-Roman (Hellenistic) influence
Realistic human figures with detailed drapery
Main subject: Buddha in human form
Use of grey stone and stucco

notes.heading: Mathura School of Art
points: Developed in Mathura region (Uttar Pradesh)
Indigenous Indian style with red sandstone
Depicted Buddha, Jain Tirthankaras, and Hindu deities
Less realistic, more symbolic representation
Strong royal and spiritual themes

notes.heading: Rock-Cut Architecture Development
points: Continued expansion of cave architecture
Ajanta Caves (early phase under Satavahanas)
Karle Caves with Chaitya halls
Bhaja and Bedsa caves in Maharashtra
Buddhist monasteries (Viharas) and prayer halls (Chaityas)

notes.heading: Important Features for UPSC

Growth of Mahayana Buddhism under Kushanas
Development of rock-cut caves in Deccan
Increased use of human representation of Buddha

notes.heading: Overview
points: Gupta Period (c. 320 CE – 550 CE) is known as the 'Golden Age of India'
Major cultural development in art, architecture, literature, and science
Strong patronage of Hinduism, along with Buddhism and Jainism
Marked refinement in temple architecture and sculpture
High level of artistic standard and classical style development

notes.heading: Key Features of Gupta Art
points: Classical and refined artistic expression
Balance, harmony, and idealized human forms
Less use of foreign influence compared to Post-Mauryan period
Development of Hindu temple architecture
Use of symbolism and spiritual representation in art

notes.heading: Gupta Sculpture
points: Highly refined and idealized human figures
Smooth, elegant body forms with spiritual expression
Buddha images from Sarnath school are most famous
Use of sandstone and bronze materials
Depiction of Hindu gods like Vishnu, Shiva, and Durga

notes.heading: Schools of Gupta Art
points: Sarnath School – Buddhist art with serene Buddha images
Mathura School (continued influence) – Hindu and Jain images
Ajanta Paintings – mural paintings depicting Jataka tales
Ellora (early phase influence) – rock-cut developments
Distinct classical Indian artistic identity developed

notes.heading: Gupta Temple Architecture
points: Beginning of structural temple architecture in India
Simple square plan with flat roofs in early stages
Development of Shikhara (tower) in later phase
Garbhagriha (sanctum) became central feature
Examples: Dashavatara Temple (Deogarh), Bhitargaon Temple

notes.heading: Ajanta Paintings
points: Located in Maharashtra
Buddhist cave paintings from Gupta period
Depict Jataka tales and life of Buddha
Use of natural colors and expressive human figures
Highly advanced mural painting technique

notes.heading: Materials and Techniques
points: Stone sculptures (sandstone and granite)
Use of fresco painting technique in Ajanta
Bronze casting also developed
Fine detailing and smooth finish in sculptures
Religious symbolism emphasized over realism

notes.heading: Important Features for UPSC

Sarnath Buddha = most iconic Gupta sculpture style

notes.heading: Overview
points: Khajuraho Temples were built between 950 CE – 1050 CE by the Chandela dynasty
Located in present-day Madhya Pradesh
Famous for Nagara style temple architecture
Originally 85 temples, only about 25 survive today
Recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

notes.heading: Chandela Dynasty Patronage
points: Built under Chandela rulers like Yasovarman and Dhanga
Chandela kings were followers of both Hinduism and Jainism
Temples reflect religious tolerance and artistic prosperity
Khajuraho was a major cultural and religious center
Decline began after 13th century due to invasions

notes.heading: Architectural Style
points: Built in Nagara style of North Indian temple architecture
High raised platform (Jagati)
Curvilinear Shikhara (tower)
Use of sandstone without mortar (dry masonry)
Temples arranged in geometric harmony

notes.heading: Structure of Temples
points: Garbhagriha (sanctum) – main deity placed here
Mandapa (hall) – assembly hall for devotees
Ardhamandapa – entrance porch
Shikhara – towering superstructure
Amalaka and Kalasha – crown elements of temple

notes.heading: Famous Temples at Khajuraho

Lakshmana Temple – dedicated to Vishnu
Vishvanatha Temple – important Shiva temple
Parsvanatha Temple – Jain temple
Chausath Yogini Temple – earliest surviving temple in Khajuraho

notes.heading: Sculptural Features

Depiction of gods, goddesses, celestial beings
Famous for erotic sculptures symbolizing kama (desire)
Scenes from daily life, music, dance, and warfare
Represents integration of spiritual and material life

notes.heading: Religious Significance

Represents Tantric traditions and spiritual symbolism
Erotic sculptures not central but symbolic of life energy
Blend of devotion, art, and philosophy
Reflects liberal and inclusive religious culture of Chandela period

notes.heading: Overview
points: Odisha temples represent the Nagara style of North Indian temple architecture with regional variation
Developed mainly between 7th to 13th century CE
Built by rulers of Kalinga region (Somavamsi, Eastern Ganga dynasty)
Famous for intricate stone carvings and towering structures
Important temple cities: Bhubaneswar, Puri, Konark

notes.heading: Kalinga School of Architecture
points: Regional sub-style of Nagara architecture
Known for vertical emphasis and elaborate ornamentation
Three main components: Rekha Deula, Pidha Deula, Khakhara Deula
Temples built using sandstone and laterite
Highly detailed exterior sculptures compared to interiors

notes.heading: Temple Structure in Odisha Style
points: Rekha Deula – sanctum with tall curvilinear shikhara
Pidha Deula – assembly hall with stepped pyramidal roof
Khakhara Deula – semi-arched structure, often for Shakti worship
Jagamohana – assembly hall in front of sanctum
Natamandira and Bhogamandapa added in later temples

notes.heading: Konark Sun Temple
points: Built by King Narasimhadeva I (13th century CE)
Dedicated to Sun God (Surya)
Designed as a giant chariot with 24 wheels and 7 horses
UNESCO World Heritage Site
Known as 'Black Pagoda' due to dark stone structure

notes.heading: Jagannath Temple, Puri
points: Built by Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva
Dedicated to Lord Jagannath (form of Vishnu)
Famous for Rath Yatra festival
Non-Hindus are not allowed inside temple
Major pilgrimage site of Char Dham

notes.heading: Lingaraja Temple, Bhubaneswar
points: Dedicated to Lord Shiva (Harihara form)
One of the finest examples of Kalinga architecture
Combines Rekha Deula and Pidha Deula styles
Built during Somavamsi dynasty
Represents maturity of Odisha temple architecture

notes.heading: Sculptural Features
points: Highly detailed exterior carvings
Depiction of gods, dancers, animals, and daily life scenes
Erotic sculptures present but less prominent than Khajuraho
Emphasis on vertical rhythm and symmetry
Use of symbolic motifs like lotus, wheels, and animals

notes.heading: Important Features for UPSC

Jagannath Temple = major Vaishnavite pilgrimage site

notes.heading: Overview

Important centers: Modhera, Patan, Mount Abu, Somnath

Strong support for temple building and Jain architecture

Gujarat became major cultural and trade hub

notes.heading: Overview
points: Indian temple architecture is broadly classified into three main schools

Each school developed distinct structural, artistic, and regional features
Evolution influenced by geography, dynasties, and cultural traditions
These schools form the core of UPSC Art & Culture syllabus

notes.heading: Nagara Style (North Indian Temple Architecture)
points: Developed in North India from 5th century CE onwards
Characterized by beehive-shaped curvilinear shikhara (tower)
No large boundary walls or gateways like gopurams
Garbhagriha (sanctum) is the most important part
Examples: Khajuraho temples, Konark Sun Temple, Odisha temples

notes.heading: Key Features of Nagara Style
points: Latina shikhara (curved tower)
Absence of elaborate boundary walls
Emphasis on vertical elevation
Multiple subsidiary shrines in complex temples
Rich sculptural decoration on exterior walls

notes.heading: Dravida Style (South Indian Temple Architecture)
points: Developed under Pallavas and perfected by Cholas, Pandyas, Vijayanagar, and Nayakas
Characterized by pyramid-shaped vimana over sanctum
Presence of massive gopurams (gateway towers)
Enclosed temple complexes with concentric walls
Examples: Brihadeeswarar Temple, Meenakshi Temple, Hampi temples

notes.heading: Key Features of Dravida Style
points: Pyramidal vimana structure
Tall and ornate gopurams
Large temple complexes (temple cities)
Use of granite stone
Strong integration of religion, economy, and society

notes.heading: Vesara Style (Hybrid Architecture)
points: Developed in Deccan region (Karnataka and parts of Andhra Pradesh)
Blend of Nagara and Dravida architectural elements
Associated mainly with Chalukyas and Hoysalas
More intricate carvings and star-shaped temple plans
Examples: Hoysaleswara Temple, Pattadakal temples

notes.heading: Key Features of Vesara Style
points: Combination of curvilinear shikhara and pyramidal vimana
Highly detailed sculptural work
Star-shaped or stellate platform design
Use of soapstone (chloritic schist)
Balanced fusion of northern and southern styles

notes.heading: Comparison of Three Styles

Dravida: Focus on gopuram and vimana
